items.abstract: Contemporary social epistemology struggles to explain cases of deep disagreement that persist despite evidence-sharing and rational deliberation. Existing approaches, including hinge epistemology and social-ontological accounts, illuminate the role of fundamental commitments but do not fully explain why certain disagreements generate structural instability rather than stable pluralism. We develop a structural account of legitimacy boundaries grounded in the functional role of non-negotiable normative commitments, using a framework that distinguishes three axes: negotiability, target scope, and actionability. Our central result, the Legitimacy Trilemma, is a structural limit: once a violation of a universal, non-negotiable legitimacy norm is publicly acknowledged within a community, the community cannot simultaneously maintain universal standards, insider inclusion, and the absence of acknowledged internal contradiction. It must instead make a repair move —excluding the violator, enforcing compliance, revising the norm, or blocking acknowledgment of the breach. This constraint is independent of the merits: it holds whether the norm is just or unjust and whether the challenge is warranted or baseless, identifying a structural form without delivering a normative verdict. The instability of deep disagreement therefore arises not primarily from irrationality or bias, but from this constraint on admissibility within shared epistemic spaces. We further argue that a specific subclass of phenomena commonly described as epistemic injustice can be modeled as such reactive boundary defense—complementary to, not a replacement for, accounts of oppression as a constitutive feature of social structures. Where deep disagreement appears intractable, the difficulty is typically not that no resolution exists but that every resolution exacts a cost—to identity, inclusion, or coherence—even among competent, good-faith agents.
items.title: Deep Disagreement and the Impossibility of Quiet Legitimacy

items.abstract: In a recent paper, De Brigard ( 2017 , Philosophical Explorations ) argues that a successful neuroscientific account of “cognitive system” needs to capture the fact that brains change over time (i.e., exhibit diachronic dynamicity ) even when these changes do not affect their functional profile (i.e., exhibit functional stability ). Unfortunately, in that paper, he fails to offer a satisfactory account that can capture both features. To fill that gap, the current paper offers a graph-theoretic strategy to characterize cognitive systems in a way that captures both diachronic dynamicity and functional stability. Specifically, it is suggested that cognitive systems can be characterized by way of employing a multi-scale modular approach in which time is parametrized.
items.title: Characterizing Dynamic Cognitive Systems

items.abstract: As a regulatory agency of the United States government, the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) is entrusted with the mission of preserving public health through ensuring the safety, effectiveness, and security of drugs, biologic products, and medical devices. Over the past decade, the healthcare sector turned increasingly to the growing sector of technological strategies for providing services. In addition, increasingly using telemedicine to facilitate care, there was an embrace of artificial intelligence (AI) enabled devices to support access and clinical decision making. These technologies have several social and physical health benefits for patients, especially those for whom access to healthcare facilities may be particularly challenging. Yet despite these benefits, there are also concerns about the safety and effectiveness of these tools, both generally, and for patients who are underrepresented in clinical research, concerns that must be addressed through regulation. This paper focuses on the FDA’s oversight of the development and regulation of AI-enabled medical devices. We argue the FDA should incorporate justice-relevant considerations of inclusion, transparency, and epistemic justice into its safety and effectiveness evaluations of AI-enabled medical devices. These considerations address concerns of inequity in AI development, ensure adequate information is relayed to the public for safe use, and promote the treatment of patients as credible sources of their own personal health to ensure that AI-enabled medical devices are safe and effective tools for patients and providers.
items.title: Embedding justice in the regulation of AI-enabled medical devices: a task for the FDA

items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence is advancing rapidly in K–12 education, outpacing existing academic policies and prompting states to issue new guidance. Across these documents, “ethics” is invoked frequently, yet its meaning in the context of AI and its translation into practice remains unsettled. This study analyzes current U.S. state-level AI policies and guidance for K–12 to identify dominant ethical frames and to assess how stated commitments are operationalized into actionable expectations for schools, educators, and vendors. By capturing early, system-level responses to generative AI, the study establishes a baseline for ethics in the AI era. To complement this largely top-down approach, which often extends pre-AI ethics lenses, the study proposes an “ethics-in-use” approach—a bottom-up strategy that employs concrete artifacts, such as policies, checklists, assignment-level AI statements, and vendor-vetting notes, that can be implemented, tested, and iteratively improved at district and classroom levels. Bridging these approaches can support a comprehensive, practical framework for conceiving and enacting ethics in K–12 AI adoption.
items.title: Ethics in the AI age: a study of state-level K–12 artificial intelligence policy frameworks in the United States

items.abstract: In this article, we discuss ‘ELSA in the Field’, building on ELSA, i.e. taking into account various Ethical, Legal, and Societal Aspects of AI systems during development and deployment, and on Responsible Innovation (RI), i.e. a framework for addressing ethical and social concerns, through anticipation, reflexivity, inclusion, and responsiveness. The ‘ELSA in the Field’ approach involves a combination of desk research and field research, and aims to facilitate collaboration between ELSA/RI experts and relevant stakeholders to learn from their expertise, understand their contexts and practices, and identify their concerns, ambitions and questions. Critically, the fieldwork is focused on specific practices , involving the deployment of diverse technologies, e.g., of AI systems. The ethical, legal, societal, and technological aspects related to these specific practices are studied, so that technological aspects are on equal footing with ethical, legal, and societal aspects. This facilitates collaboration between ELSA/RI experts and technology-oriented people. The ‘ELSA in the Field’ is introduced and positioned relative to ELSA and RI. It is then described in practical terms and with examples from a research and innovation project in which the authors collaborate. The article closes with a discussion of participation, iteration, reflexivity, and boundary objects.
items.title: ELSA in the field: studying ethical, legal, societal, and technological aspects of artificial intelligence in practice

items.abstract: Abstract Large language model-based agents are increasingly being integrated into core battlefield functions, including intelligence analysis, data fusion, and battlefield management. This paper argues that the very features that make such agents operationally attractive, namely their capacity for initiative, interpretation, their goal-directedness, and dynamic memory, are the same features that render context-appropriate human judgment and control substantively ineffectual in those parts of the kill chain where agents operate. Drawing on specific use cases, the paper argues that by relocating initiative and interpretation, LLM-based agents displace human decision-making in ways that makes their use incompatible with the requirement of human judgment and control which is central to existing governance frameworks, like those proposed by the Group of Governmental Experts of the Convention on Certain Conventional Weapons (GGE-CCW) and the Responsible AI in the Military Domain Summit (REAIM). The paper concludes that a subset of agentic AI applications, particularly those deployed for data fusion and battlefield management in lethal contexts, cannot be used justifiably on the battlefield under current and foreseeable conditions, and proposes two ways for the international governance community to respond to this challenge.
items.title: The end of human judgment in the kill chain? Relocating initiative and interpretation with agentic AI

items.abstract: In October 2025, the UK Competition Appeal Tribunal (CAT) handed down its landmark decision on Kent v Apple . 1 The Tribunal ruled that Apple had abused its dominant position through both exclusionary practices and charging excessive prices. Specifically, the Tribunal found that Apple’s 30 per cent commission charged to app developers went beyond mere overcharging, operating as an unlawful form of economic exploitation. 2 Consequently, Apple was ordered to pay approximately £1.5 billion in damages to UK customers. In contrast to prior investigations conducted by the European Commission and US Courts, which were narrowly focused on Apple’s anti-steering policies, the Tribunal grabbed the bull by the horns and directly addressed whether Apple’s commission rate was excessive and unfair. As such, Kent marks a major analytical milestone in how competition law operationalises the concept of ‘fair profits’.
items.title: Reassessing competition law’s fair profit doctrine in the era of Big Tech: Towards an integrated profitability framework

items.abstract: Abstract This article critically engages with Ben Judah’s Briançon chapter to interrogate the normalisation of violence within EU migration governance. Using the journey of Brico and his family as an analytical lens, it demonstrates how EU externalisation policies extend far beyond territorial borders, shaping migratory trajectories through legal, political, and economic interventions in third countries such as Niger and Libya. The first part situates Brico’s experiences within the broader framework of EU cooperation agreements, anti-smuggling laws, and maritime interception practices, highlighting their material consequences, including increased precarity, exploitation, and exposure to systemic human rights violations. The second part examines how such violence becomes normalised within European legal and political consciousness. It argues that this normalisation is sustained through processes of dehumanisation, the construction of hierarchies of deservingness, and the diffusion of responsibility. Drawing on jurisprudence from European courts, the article exposes persistent gaps in accountability, particularly in the context of extraterritorialised border control. It further reflects on the ethical tensions inherent in narrating migrant suffering, questioning whether such representations challenge or inadvertently reproduce the very structures they seek to critique. Ultimately, the article contends that EU migration governance produces a form of “everyday dystopia” in which systemic violence is both obscured and rendered routine. By foregrounding the lived realities behind legal frameworks, it calls for a re-examination of the relationship between sovereignty, accountability, and human rights in contemporary migration law.
items.title: Everyday dystopia: EU migration governance and its normalisation – reading ‘Briançon’

items.abstract: Abstract The literature on epistemic violence and its remedies has seen significant growth in recent decades. Meanwhile, within the epistemological literature, a smaller but growing number of proposals come from the intersection between epistemology and care ethics. This paper aims to bring these two bodies of literature into conversation by identifying a specific type of epistemic care that I call “resistant epistemic care” (REC). After analyzing some existing proposals for “epistemic care” in the first section, I set out my own account of REC as an especially resistant and creative capacity to restore the epistemic agency and contributions of victims of epistemic violence even in the face of conditions of severe epistemic obscurity. Next I argue that REC can fruitfully provide a framework to confront epistemic violence, and offer the Spanish “La Manada” (the “Wolf-Pack”) and its feminist response in the “#YoTeCreo” (“#IBelieveYou”) movement as a case study to demonstrate how REC helps overcome the epistemic violence suffered by victims of sexual assault by generating hermeneutical change at the collective level.
items.title: “I Believe You, Sister”: Epistemic Violence, Epistemic Care, and the “Wolf-Pack”

items.abstract: Abstract Investment returns are a key determinant of long-run inequality. Financial markets tend to reward investors who bear more risk with higher expected returns. We argue, on Dworkinian luck egalitarian grounds, that the resulting inequality is unjust: risk appetites are largely a matter of brute luck, yet in societies with financial markets the capacity to bear risk is a personal resource. Risk aversion is not an ‘expensive taste’, and nothing turns on the rationality of risk appetites. The state has moral reasons to function as the egalitarian risk-taker of last resort.
items.title: Risk appetites, investment returns, and distributive justice

items.abstract: Abstract This article examines Congress’s continuing role in implementing Title VII of the Civil Rights Act of 1964. Although scholarship has emphasized the importance of judicial interpretation, administrative development, and private litigation in transforming Title VII into one of the most consequential components of the modern civil-rights state, Congress remained deeply engaged in determining how the statute would be enforced. Between 1965 and 1972, lawmakers repeatedly debated proposals to strengthen the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC), ultimately constructing an enforcement regime centered on federal litigation rather than administrative cease-and-desist authority. The article then traces Congress’s response to the Supreme Court’s 1988 and 1989 Title VII decisions, showing that the Civil Rights Acts of 1990 and 1991 were principally efforts to restore the enforcement framework that lawmakers believed the Court had unsettled. Taken together, these episodes demonstrate that implementation was not a discrete stage following enactment, but an ongoing process of institutional negotiation among Congress, the presidency, the courts, and the administrative state. Recovering Congress’s role in these post-enactment struggles broadens our understanding of Title VII’s development and illuminates the changing politics of civil-rights enforcement after 1964.
items.title: Congress and the Making of the Title VII Enforcement Regime, 1965–1991

items.journal: Critical Review of International Social and Political Philosophy
items.title: Political integration and the majority

items.abstract: Abstract This paper introduces and offers a solution to an under-explored problem for Rawls’s account of intergenerational justice; specifically, for the just savings principle. This principle requires each generation to save at a net-positive rate until society has sufficient material resources to establish just institutions, after which it permits a net-zero rate resulting in economic stationarity. This involves a sharp drop in the savings rate from the last pre-transition generation to the first post-transition generation, and is thus unacceptable to the parties in the original position. Why? Rawls insists any savings principle must seem fair to both sides of each pair of adjacent generations, but the sharp drop would not seem fair to the last pre-transition generation. My solution tapers the savings rate down to net-zero once just institutions are established. This principle is both acceptable to the parties and allows Rawls to maintain the compatibility of justice with economic stationarity.
items.title: The Transition to Justice: A New Problem for the Just Savings Principle

items.abstract: Abstract Climate change contributes to democratic upheaval, and the slow and unpredictable passage of the democratic process can appear ill-suited to the urgent demands of the climate crisis. In consequence, climate-conscious NGOs and environmental defenders are increasingly turning away from traditional liberal democratic processes, instead mobilising litigation and civil disobedience to effect legal change. However, these phenomena can be seen as democratically troubling, contributing to legal disruption. The UNECE Aarhus Convention—a hybrid environmental human rights instrument—is a rich repository of legal rights and democratic ambition that can help its parties to navigate the democratic and legal challenges of the climate crisis. Using the examples of climate litigation and civil disobedience, I show that the Convention is a dynamic and responsive legal instrument that speaks to the troubles posed by climate disruption, promoting an expansive understanding of democratic engagement and providing its parties with a blueprint to navigate these phenomena well.
items.title: The Democratic Troubles of the Climate Crisis and the Aarhus Convention

items.abstract: ABSTRACT We are seeing increasing work in bioethics to defend and define an ethical duty to minimise healthcare's environmental impacts. So far, the duty is often defined in terms of reducing healthcare's greenhouse gas emissions and two positions have emerged on whether and what limits to the duty apply: soft exceptionalism and non‐exceptionalism. Yet, the philosophical grounds for the duty to minimise healthcare's environmental impacts are often not well explained or clearly articulated. That matters because, as this paper argues, different philosophical grounds generate different understandings of the duty's content and limits. In particular, this paper focuses on the implications of using different justice ‐based grounds for the duty. Section I first establishes that different axes of justice—social, environmental, ecological—can each be used to ground a general duty to minimise healthcare's environmental impacts. Section II shows that a range of ontologies underlie the conceptions of justice encompassed within those axes. Section III then demonstrates that the selected axis of justice and underlying ontology affects the nature—limits and content—of the resultant duty to minimise healthcare's environmental impacts. Ultimately, numerous different ways to understand the duty's limits and content are shown to exist. Many of those understandings require more than reducing healthcare's greenhouse gas emissions, and not all are consistent with soft exceptionalism or non‐exceptionalism. To conclude, the paper considers whether reasons exist for favouring certain interpretations of the duty over others.
items.title: Towards Clarifying the Duty to Minimise Healthcare's Environmental Impacts

items.abstract: ABSTRACT It has recently been proposed that fine‐tuned large‐language models (LLMs) could more accurately predict the preferences of incapacitated patients than surrogates. This hypothetical technology has been named the personalised patient preference predictor (P4). Advocates of the P4 claim that the P4 will not only more accurately predict patient preferences, but will better respect patient autonomy, facilitate the composition of advance directives, and reduce the emotional burden of surrogate decision‐making. I challenge these purported benefits by arguing that the P4 would pose a substantive risk to our ability to meaningfully grapple with death. Drawing on the philosophies of Søren Kierkegaard and Martin Heidegger, I argue that adopting an existential attitude towards death is central to the pursuit of an ethical life. Implementation of the P4 risks inhibiting both patients and surrogates from adopting an existential attitude towards death, with deleterious consequences.
items.title: Death, Existentialism, and the Personalised Patient Preference Predictor

items.abstract: ABSTRACT In this paper, I use some important insights from the literature on the conflict of rights to reconsider the conflict of rights in some unwanted pregnancies. Specifically, I reconsider antiabortion arguments that rely on the premise that the fetus's right to life is more stringent than, and so overrides, the pregnant person's right to their body. I argue that, if this is so (and I do not believe it is), then the pregnant person's right to their body is infringed (not violated). This mere infringement, however, generates a duty on the part of the fetus to compensate the pregnant person for the unwanted use of their body. I argue that neither Catholic nor philosophical views on filial duties provide an adequate solution to the question of compensation.
items.title: Compensation and Unwanted Pregnancy
